XIV.
The Meeting


“My beloved child,” he resumed, “was now growing rapidly worse. The
physician who attended her had failed to produce the slightest
impression on her disease, for such I then supposed it to be. He saw my
alarm, and suggested a consultation. I called in an abler physician,
from Gratz.

Several days elapsed before he arrived. He was a good and pious, as
well as a learned man. Having seen my poor ward together, they withdrew
to my library to confer and discuss. I, from the adjoining room, where
I awaited their summons, heard these two gentlemen’s voices raised in
something sharper than a strictly philosophical discussion. I knocked
at the door and entered. I found the old physician from Gratz
maintaining his theory. His rival was combating it with undisguised
ridicule, accompanied with bursts of laughter. This unseemly
manifestation subsided and the altercation ended on my entrance.

“‘Sir,’ said my first physician,’my learned brother seems to think that
you want a conjuror, and not a doctor.’

“‘Pardon me,’ said the old physician from Gratz, looking displeased, ‘I
shall state my own view of the case in my own way another time. I
grieve, Monsieur le General, that by my skill and science I can be of
no use.

Before I go I shall do myself the honor to suggest something to you.’

“He seemed thoughtful, and sat down at a table and began to write.

Profoundly disappointed, I made my bow, and as I turned to go, the
other doctor pointed over his shoulder to his companion who was
writing, and then, with a shrug, significantly touched his forehead.

“This consultation, then, left me precisely where I was. I walked out
into the grounds, all but distracted. The doctor from Gratz, in ten or
fifteen minutes, overtook me. He apologized for having followed me, but
said that he could not conscientiously take his leave without a few
words more. He told me that he could not be mistaken; no natural
disease exhibited the same symptoms; and that death was already very
near. There remained, however, a day, or possibly two, of life. If the
fatal seizure were at once arrested, with great care and skill her
strength might possibly return. But all hung now upon the confines of
the irrevocable. One more assault might extinguish the last spark of
vitality which is, every moment, ready to die.

“‘And what is the nature of the seizure you speak of?’ I entreated.

“‘I have stated all fully in this note, which I place in your hands
upon the distinct condition that you send for the nearest clergyman,
and open my letter in his presence, and on no account read it till he
is with you; you would despise it else, and it is a matter of life and
death. Should the priest fail you, then, indeed, you may read it.’

“He asked me, before taking his leave finally, whether I would wish to
see a man curiously learned upon the very subject, which, after I had
read his letter, would probably interest me above all others, and he
urged me earnestly to invite him to visit him there; and so took his
leave.

“The ecclesiastic was absent, and I read the letter by myself. At
another time, or in another case, it might have excited my ridicule.
But into what quackeries will not people rush for a last chance, where
all accustomed means have failed, and the life of a beloved object is
at stake?

“Nothing, you will say, could be more absurd than the learned man’s
letter.

It was monstrous enough to have consigned him to a madhouse. He said
that the patient was suffering from the visits of a vampire! The
punctures which she described as having occurred near the throat, were,
he insisted, the insertion of those two long, thin, and sharp teeth
which, it is well known, are peculiar to vampires; and there could be
no doubt, he added, as to the well-defined presence of the small livid
mark which all concurred in describing as that induced by the demon’s
lips, and every symptom described by the sufferer was in exact
conformity with those recorded in every case of a similar visitation.

“Being myself wholly skeptical as to the existence of any such portent
as the vampire, the supernatural theory of the good doctor furnished,
in my opinion, but another instance of learning and intelligence oddly
associated with some one hallucination. I was so miserable, however,
that, rather than try nothing, I acted upon the instructions of the
letter.

“I concealed myself in the dark dressing room, that opened upon the
poor patient’s room, in which a candle was burning, and watched there
till she was fast asleep. I stood at the door, peeping through the
small crevice, my sword laid on the table beside me, as my directions
prescribed, until, a little after one, I saw a large black object, very
ill-defined, crawl, as it seemed to me, over the foot of the bed, and
swiftly spread itself up to the poor girl’s throat, where it swelled,
in a moment, into a great, palpitating mass.

“For a few moments I had stood petrified. I now sprang forward, with my
sword in my hand. The black creature suddenly contracted towards the
foot of the bed, glided over it, and, standing on the floor about a
yard below the foot of the bed, with a glare of skulking ferocity and
horror fixed on me, I saw Millarca. Speculating I know not what, I
struck at her instantly with my sword; but I saw her standing near the
door, unscathed. Horrified, I pursued, and struck again. She was gone;
and my sword flew to shivers against the door.

“I can’t describe to you all that passed on that horrible night. The
whole house was up and stirring. The specter Millarca was gone. But her
victim was sinking fast, and before the morning dawned, she died.”

The old General was agitated. We did not speak to him. My father walked
to some little distance, and began reading the inscriptions on the
tombstones; and thus occupied, he strolled into the door of a side
chapel to prosecute his researches. The General leaned against the
wall, dried his eyes, and sighed heavily. I was relieved on hearing the
voices of Carmilla and Madame, who were at that moment approaching. The
voices died away.

In this solitude, having just listened to so strange a story,
connected, as it was, with the great and titled dead, whose monuments
were moldering among the dust and ivy round us, and every incident of
which bore so awfully upon my own mysterious case—in this haunted spot,
darkened by the towering foliage that rose on every side, dense and
high above its noiseless walls—a horror began to steal over me, and my
heart sank as I thought that my friends were, after all, not about to
enter and disturb this triste and ominous scene.

The old General’s eyes were fixed on the ground, as he leaned with his
hand upon the basement of a shattered monument.

Under a narrow, arched doorway, surmounted by one of those demoniacal
grotesques in which the cynical and ghastly fancy of old Gothic carving
delights, I saw very gladly the beautiful face and figure of Carmilla
enter the shadowy chapel.

I was just about to rise and speak, and nodded smiling, in answer to
her peculiarly engaging smile; when with a cry, the old man by my side
caught up the woodman’s hatchet, and started forward. On seeing him a
brutalized change came over her features. It was an instantaneous and
horrible transformation, as she made a crouching step backwards. Before
I could utter a scream, he struck at her with all his force, but she
dived under his blow, and unscathed, caught him in her tiny grasp by
the wrist. He struggled for a moment to release his arm, but his hand
opened, the axe fell to the ground, and the girl was gone.

He staggered against the wall. His grey hair stood upon his head, and a
moisture shone over his face, as if he were at the point of death.

The frightful scene had passed in a moment. The first thing I recollect
after, is Madame standing before me, and impatiently repeating again
and again, the question, “Where is Mademoiselle Carmilla?”

I answered at length, “I don’t know—I can’t tell—she went there,” and I
pointed to the door through which Madame had just entered; “only a
minute or two since.”

“But I have been standing there, in the passage, ever since
Mademoiselle Carmilla entered; and she did not return.”

She then began to call “Carmilla,” through every door and passage and
from the windows, but no answer came.

“She called herself Carmilla?” asked the General, still agitated.

“Carmilla, yes,” I answered.

“Aye,” he said; “that is Millarca. That is the same person who long ago
was called Mircalla, Countess Karnstein. Depart from this accursed
ground, my poor child, as quickly as you can. Drive to the clergyman’s
house, and stay there till we come. Begone! May you never behold
Carmilla more; you will not find her here.”
generated_text:
The General’s knuckles blanched white where he clamped down on the carved head of his walking stick, cold graveyard moss seeping through his breeches as he leaned in, his voice frayed thin with decades-old grief. “My beloved ward was wasting away by the hour. The local physician bled her, dosed her, and every symptom grew worse: dark bruise-like circles bloomed under her eyes no matter how much she slept, she woke screaming at dawn gasping that something cold had fastened to her throat, two tiny pricks oozing slow, thick blood he could not explain. He saw I was half mad with fear, and suggested a consultation with a more learned man from Gratz.

It was three days before that old physician arrived, pious and sharp, his coat dusted with road grime. The two men examined my girl together, then withdrew to my library to confer, leaving me pacing the next room, waiting. Their voices rose, not in calm debate, but in something sharp, ugly: the local doctor cackling, snorting, sneering at the older man’s theory. I banged on the door and stepped in, and the laughter died on his lips.
“Sir,” the local physician said, nodding mockingly at his peer, “my learned friend seems to think you need a conjuror, not a doctor.”
“Pardon me,” the Gratz doctor said, his face tight with quiet fury, “I will state my case properly elsewhere. I grieve, General, that my science can do nothing for your child. But before I leave, I must write you something that cannot wait.”

He sat at the table, scribbling furiously. When I turned to leave, the other doctor jerked his thumb over his shoulder at the writing man, tapped his own forehead with a smirk, and shrugged. The consultation had left me no further ahead than I started. I wandered out into the overgrown park, half distracted, ready to scream, when the old Gratz physician caught up with me ten minutes later. He apologized for following, said he could not in good conscience leave before he warned me.
“There is no natural disease that matches her symptoms,” he said, his voice low, urgent. “She has a day, maybe two, left to live. One more visit from what haunts her, and the last spark of her life will be snuffed out forever.”
“What visit?” I begged him.
“I have written every detail in this note,” he said, pressing the sealed paper into my hand. “You are not to open it until the nearest clergyman stands at your side. If you read it alone, you will think me a madman, and this is a matter of life and death. If the priest is away, then you may break the seal.”

Before he left, he urged me to send for a man he knew, a scholar who had spent his life studying exactly the strange affliction laid out in that letter, and pressed me to waste no time. But the priest was off visiting a dying parishioner, miles away. I broke the seal alone. Any other day, any other circumstance, I would have laughed the letter off as the raving of a lunatic. But when every cure has failed, and the life of the person you love most is hanging by a thread, you grasp at even the most impossible straws.

The letter said she was being preyed on by a vampire. Those two tiny pricks at her throat? The marks of the creature’s long, sharp fangs. The livid, bruised ring around the wounds? The trace of the demon’s lips. Every one of her waking nightmares, every lurch of her fading pulse, matched every recorded case of vampire visitation to the letter. I still did not believe such a thing could exist. I thought the good old doctor had gone senile, that some odd hallucination had warped his years of learning. But I could not do nothing. I followed his instructions to the letter.

I hid in the dark dressing room that opened off her bedchamber, a single tallow candle guttering on her nightstand. My sword lay on the small table beside my post, just as the note ordered. I peered through the crack in the door, watched her fall asleep, until just after one in the morning, I saw it: a great, shapeless black mass, crawling slow over the foot of her bed, oozing upward until it spread over her throat, swelling into a great, throbbing, palpitating lump, as if it was feeding on her very life. I stood petrified for a long, cold heartbeat. Then I burst through the door, sword raised high. The black creature recoiled, fast as a striking snake, glided off the bed, and stood on the stone floor a yard from her bed foot. It was Millarca. Her eyes burned with that skulking, feral, inhuman glare, fixed right on me. I swung my sword with all my strength. The blade passed right through empty air. She was standing by the bedroom door, unharmed, a smile tugging at her lips. I screamed, lunged again. She was gone. My sword shattered against the oak door in a spray of steel splinters.

I cannot tell you the full horror of that night. The whole house woke, servants stumbling through the halls with lanterns, screaming. The specter Millarca was nowhere to be found. But my ward was sinking fast. Before the first pale streak of dawn painted the sky, she was dead.”

The General fell silent, his shoulders heaving. None of us spoke. My father wandered a few paces off, squinting at the moss-choked inscriptions carved into the weathered tombstones, before stepping through the arch of a side chapel to read the carvings on the old sarcophagi inside. The General leaned against the cracked base of a broken monument, wiping tears from his face with a shaking hand, and sighed so heavy it sounded like a death rattle.

I thought I heard Carmilla and Madame’s voices approaching from the path, but the sound died away before they came into view. The graveyard was wrapped in thick, oppressive shadow, the oak and ivy canopy so dense not a sliver of sun touched the flagstones under our feet. The air smelled of turned earth and rot, and a cold dread crept over my skin, settling in my bones. The story the General had just told was too close, too familiar, matching every strange, waking nightmare I had lived these past months. I waited for Carmilla and Madame to step through the arch, but no one came.

Then I saw her. Under the narrow arched doorway of the chapel, crowned by a leering, grotesque gargoyle carved in that old Gothic style, its face twisted into a cynical, hungry grin, Carmilla stepped into the dim light. Her face was soft and beautiful, her smile warm, that peculiarly engaging curl to her lips that always made my pulse flutter. I lifted my hand to wave, about to stand and greet her.

The General moved faster than I could follow. He snatched up the woodman’s axe that had been propped against the nearby mausoleum wall, and lunged forward with a snarl. The soft smile dropped from Carmilla’s face in a single, horrifying instant. A brutal, inhuman fury warped her features. She crouched back, hissing. Before I could even draw breath to scream, the General swung the axe with all his force at her head. She ducked under the blow, her small, ice-cold hand fastening around his wrist. He struggled to yank free, but his fingers went numb, dead, the axe clattering to the stone with a sharp, echoing crack. A blink later, she was gone.

The General staggered back against the wall, his grey hair standing on end, cold sweat dripping down his pale face like he was moments from death. The whole scene had lasted no more than three seconds. When I blinked, Madame was standing in front of me, her face tight with impatience, repeating the same question over and over.
“Where is Mademoiselle Carmilla? Where did she go?”
“I don’t know,” I stammered, pointing at the doorway she had just stepped through. “She was there, just a minute ago.”
“But I have been standing in that passage ever since she walked into the chapel,” Madame said, her voice rising in panic. “She never came back out.” She ran through every door, every corridor, calling Carmilla’s name at the top of her lungs, but no answer came. No sound but the wind hissing through the ivy.

“She called herself Carmilla?” the General said, his voice still shaking, his hand pressed to his chest to steady his breathing.
“Carmilla, yes,” I said.
“Aye,” he said, his eyes dark with ancient terror. “That is Millarca. That is the same woman who, a hundred and fifty years ago, was Mircalla, Countess Karnstein. Run, my poor child. Leave this accursed ground at once. Drive straight to the clergyman’s house, and do not stop until you are behind his doors. Stay there until we come for you. Begone. You will never find Carmilla here. May you never see her face again.”
